## Exercise 1: Distances and ordination on the species table

> As this morning, Pi writes the code and you decide what it means. An
> ordination is easy to produce and easy to over-read: a clean split on a plot
> invites a story about axis 1. This exercise asks you to get the numbers
> behind each story before you believe it.

Open `notebooks/03-ordination.qmd`, run the setup chunk, and start Pi with a
fresh conversation. The setup chunk builds `ps_species` and `ps_genes` and
attaches your `community` column to both. Tell Pi to use those objects rather
than building new ones.

### Part 1: Predict

1. Bray-Curtis uses abundances. Jaccard uses only presence and absence. Our
   species table is about 89% zeros. Which of the two do you expect to separate
   the two community types more clearly, and why?
2. If you shuffled the `outcome` label randomly across all 471 samples, what
   `R2` would PERMANOVA report? Give a number.
3. One sample has 438 reads. Where do you expect it to sit in a Bray-Curtis
   ordination?

### Part 2: Ask, look, decide

1. The first ordination:

   > Using `ps_species` from the setup chunk, make a Bray-Curtis PCoA with
   > microViz at the species level and colour it by `community`. Put the share
   > of variation on each axis title.

   Check it before you read anything into it. Ask Pi how many points are on
   the plot (there should be 471) and how many samples have no `community`
   value (there should be none). If the colours are all grey, your column did
   not attach.

2. Three distances, side by side:

   > Make the same ordination three ways, side by side: `"identity"` with
   > `"bray"`, `"binary"` with `"jaccard"`, and `"clr"` with `"euclidean"`.
   > Under them, add a scree plot for each showing the share of variation held
   > by the first eight axes.

   Compare the three with your answer to question 1. Then decide which one you
   would put in a paper and write one sentence in your notebook saying why.

3. One plot, many colourings. Ask Pi for the Bray-Curtis ordination as a grid
   of panels, coloured by `outcome`, `time_point`, `nugent`, `lacto_fraction`
   and library size. Which colouring lines up with axis 1? Which one shows
   nothing you can see by eye?

4. What is axis 1? From here on, write your own requests. Ask Pi to interpret
   your ordination. It will probably write a confident paragraph about the
   biology of axis 1. Now ask for the numbers behind it: the correlation of
   axis 1 with `lacto_fraction`, and the five genera whose abundance tracks
   axis 1 most closely, each with its correlation. Does the paragraph still
   hold up?

5. PERMANOVA. Ask for the `R2` and p-value of `community`, `outcome`,
   `time_point` and `rnaseq_batch`, as a table and as a bar chart. Check it
   against the slides: about 17.5% for community, 8.7% for visit, 0.5% for
   outcome, and an RNA batch that explains nothing here.

   Then make the null distribution yourself:

   > Shuffle the `outcome` labels across samples 20 times, run PERMANOVA on
   > each shuffled version with 99 permutations, and plot the 20 `R2` values
   > as a histogram with the real outcome `R2` marked as a line.

   How does this compare with your answer to question 2? Where does the real
   value sit?

6. Argue about the settings. The slides used `by = "margin"`. Ask Pi to run it
   again with `by = "terms"` and to put both results side by side, then to
   explain why they differ when labels are related to each other. Then ask it:
   "Each participant appears three times. Does PERMANOVA know that, and does it
   matter?" Push on the answer until you could explain it to your neighbour.

7. The 438-read sample. Ask Pi to mark it and label it on the ordination. Was
   your prediction right? Then ask for the ordination again without the
   samples you dropped this morning, side by side with the original. Did
   anything else move?

8. Polish one figure. Take the community-coloured Bray-Curtis plot and ask for
   variations: ellipses around each group, one panel per visit, point size by
   library size, lines joining each participant's three visits for ten
   participants. Keep the version that shows the most, then make it ready for
   a talk: your own colours, axis titles in words, a legend people can read,
   saved as a PNG.

### Discussion

- Which of the three distances would you publish? Defend it in one sentence.
- `community` explains a very large share of this table. Is that a finding?
- Pi's first paragraph about axis 1: what did it get right, and what did it say
  that the numbers did not support?
- Your ordination shows visit structure. Each participant appears three times.
  Does PERMANOVA know that, and does it matter?
